overview.title: The long-term vision for AI
overview.section: 19.4 The missing ingredients: Search and symbols
overview.main_topic: The authors' five-point vision of future AI: program-like models, a blend of algorithmic and geometric modules, models grown from a global library of subroutines, discrete search guided by deep-learning intuition, and human-like extreme generalization; plus a rejection of singularitarian fears.
overview.central_idea: Future AI will consist of program-like models grown automatically by a deep-learning-guided program search over a global, ever-growing library of reusable algorithmic and geometric subroutines, achieving human-like extreme generalization from little data; such a system could be called AGI, but robot-apocalypse fantasies are misguided.
overview.importance: This page is the culmination of chapter 19 and condenses the whole of section 19.4 into a checklist. It is the authors' answer to 'what comes after deep learning as we know it?'
learning_objectives: Restate each point of the long-term vision and connect it to the subsection that developed it.
Explain 'value-centric + program-centric abstraction' as a design principle.
Explain why reusable program-like primitives enable learning from very little data.
Understand the authors' position on AGI and the 'singularity'.
prerequisites: Hybrid systems and guided program search (pp.614-616).

summary:
The page finishes the long-term vision begun on p.617. Point 1 concludes: program-like models will be closer to the **abstract mental models** humans maintain about their surroundings and themselves, and will generalize more strongly thanks to their **rich algorithmic nature**.

Point 2: models will blend **algorithmic modules** (formal reasoning, search, abstraction) with **geometric modules** (informal intuition, pattern recognition), achieving a blend of **value-centric and program-centric abstraction**. AlphaGo and self-driving cars, which required much manual engineering and human design decisions, are early examples of a symbolic-geometric blend.

Point 3: models will be **grown automatically** rather than hardcoded, from modular parts in a **global library of reusable subroutines**, a library evolved by learning high-performing models on thousands of previous tasks and datasets. Frequent problem-solving patterns identified by the **meta-learning system** become reusable subroutines, like functions and classes in software engineering.

Point 4: the process that searches combinations of subroutines to grow new models will be **discrete search (program synthesis)**, heavily guided by **program-space intuition** provided by deep learning.

Point 5: the library and model-growing system will achieve a form of **human-like extreme generalization**: given a new task, it will assemble a working model using **very little data**, thanks to program-like primitives that generalize well and experience with similar tasks, just as humans quickly learn a complex new video game when they've played many others, because their models of past experience are **abstract and program-like**, not mere stimulus-action mappings.

Finally, such a **perpetually learning model-growing system** could be interpreted as **artificial general intelligence (AGI)**. But the authors dismiss any **singularitarian robot apocalypse** as pure fantasy stemming from profound misunderstandings of intelligence and technology, a critique they leave outside the book.

paragraphs.excerpt: that humans maintain about their surroundings and themselves, and they will be capable
paragraphs.what_it_says: (End of bullet 1, from p.617) Program-like models will be much closer to the abstract mental models humans maintain about their surroundings and themselves, and will generalize more strongly due to their rich algorithmic nature.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The source of better generalization is identified as *algorithmic* structure: a program that implements a rule applies it to any input, whereas a continuous mapping only covers the neighborhood of its training data (local generalization). 'Mental models of surroundings and themselves' points to structured, reusable world models rather than input-output reflexes.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It ties the vision to the chapter's diagnosis (19.1.3): deep learning models struggle to learn generalizable programs.

terminology.meaning: A structured internal representation of how the world (or oneself) works that can be used to reason and predict.

connections: p.593: deep learning's failure to learn exact addition illustrates the weak generalization of non-algorithmic models.

paragraphs.excerpt: In particular, models will blend algorithmic modules providing formal reasoning, search, and abstraction
paragraphs.what_it_says: Models will blend algorithmic modules (formal reasoning, search, abstraction) with geometric modules (informal intuition, pattern recognition), achieving a blend of value-centric and program-centric abstraction. AlphaGo or self-driving cars, which required much manual software engineering and human design decisions, are an early example of such a blend of symbolic and geometric AI.
paragraphs.what_it_means: This is the architectural principle of figure 19.15, phrased in the chapter's vocabulary: geometric modules ↔ value-centric abstraction (continuous similarity), algorithmic modules ↔ program-centric abstraction (discrete structure). The parenthetical about manual engineering repeats the caveat from p.614: today's blends are hand-made.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It is the one-sentence summary of 19.4.1-19.4.5: neither pole of abstraction suffices alone; cognition, and future AI, uses both.

terminology.meaning: Abstraction based on discrete structure: identifying exact programs/rules, enabling reasoning and planning.
AI built from explicit symbols and rules manipulated by algorithms.

connections: p.614: AlphaGo (MCTS + policy/value networks) and Waymo (3D world model + perception) introduced as hybrids.
p.615: the same blend described with figure 19.15.
p.611: 19.4.2 Cognition as a combination of both kinds of abstraction.

paragraphs.excerpt: Such models will be grown automatically rather than hardcoded by human engineers, using
paragraphs.what_it_says: Models will be grown automatically, not hardcoded, using modular parts from a global library of reusable subroutines, evolved by learning high-performing models on thousands of previous tasks and datasets. Frequent problem-solving patterns identified by the meta-learning system will become reusable subroutines, like functions and classes in software engineering, and be added to the library.
paragraphs.what_it_means: 'Grown' is a deliberate word: models aren't designed in one go but assembled and refined incrementally from parts, as in figure 19.16. The library is 'evolved': which subroutines exist is itself the outcome of selection by usefulness across thousands of tasks. Frequency is the trigger for abstraction: a pattern seen repeatedly is worth packaging.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It removes the human engineer from the loop that, on p.614, still hand-codes the algorithmic parts of hybrids.

terminology.meaning: A model assembled incrementally by an automated process from library components, rather than hand-designed.
The process that learns to build models across tasks and curates the library.

connections: p.617: figure 19.16 and the software-library analogy.
p.616: why reuse across tasks is necessary.

paragraphs.excerpt: The process that searches over possible combinations of subroutines to grow new models
paragraphs.what_it_says: The process that searches combinations of subroutines to grow new models will be discrete search (program synthesis), heavily guided by program-space intuition provided by deep learning.
paragraphs.what_it_means: This assigns roles precisely: the search engine is discrete (so its products can be exact, non-differentiable programs), and deep learning acts as its guide (to avoid combinatorial explosion). It is the second avenue of 19.4.5, applied to the library setting: the 'primitives' searched over are now high-level library subroutines, which also shortens the programs that need to be found.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It shows both avenues of p.614 converging: hybrid models are the product, guided search is the production process.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: searching over high-level library subroutines instead of low-level primitives reduces required program length $L$, and since search cost grows like $V^L$ or faster, a richer library can make previously infeasible programs reachable, even though $V$ grows.

terminology.meaning: Learned sense of which directions in the space of programs lead toward a solution.

connections: p.615: combinatorial explosion of unguided search.
p.616: deep learning learning the manifold-like structure of program space.

paragraphs.excerpt: This global subroutine library and associated model-growing system will be able to achieve
paragraphs.what_it_says: The library and model-growing system will achieve a form of human-like extreme generalization: given a new task or situation, it will assemble a working model using very little data, thanks to rich program-like primitives that generalize well and extensive experience with similar tasks. Similarly, humans quickly learn a complex new video game if they've played many previous games, because the models derived from that experience are abstract and program-like, rather than a basic mapping between stimuli and action.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Data efficiency comes from two sources: **priors** (primitives that already encode general, correct procedures) and **experience** (knowing which combinations tend to work). The video-game analogy contrasts two kinds of learned knowledge: 'press jump when an obstacle is near' (stimulus-action mapping, specific to one game) vs. 'there are enemies, collectibles, a goal; obstacles are avoided by jumping' (an abstract, program-like model that transfers to a new game with different graphics and rules).
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It defines success for the whole project in terms of extreme generalization, the concept introduced in 19.2.2 and the target behind ARC (19.3.5-19.3.7).

terminology.meaning: Adapting to radically new tasks or situations from very little data.
A direct learned association between inputs and responses, without an abstract model of the situation.

connections: p.597: 19.2.2 Local generalization vs. extreme generalization.
p.605: ARC Prize, the benchmark for on-the-fly adaptation to novel tasks.

paragraphs.excerpt: This perpetually learning model-growing system can be interpreted as an artificial general intelligence
paragraphs.what_it_says: This perpetually learning, model-growing system can be interpreted as an artificial general intelligence (AGI). But don't expect any singularitarian robot apocalypse: that's pure fantasy stemming from profound misunderstandings of both intelligence and technology, a critique that doesn't belong in this book.
paragraphs.what_it_means: AGI is defined here functionally, as a system that keeps learning and can efficiently build models for new tasks, not as a conscious agent with its own goals. The authors separate this technical notion from popular 'singularity' narratives (runaway self-improvement leading to catastrophe), which they reject without arguing the point here.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It closes chapter 19 by grounding the term AGI in the chapter's view of intelligence as efficient adaptation, and signals the authors' stance on AI risk narratives without making it the book's topic.
paragraphs.technical_idea: This is an opinion section; the dismissal of singularitarian scenarios is the authors' view and is not argued on the page.

terminology.meaning: Here: a system that can perpetually learn and grow models for new tasks with human-like generalization.
Relating to belief in a 'technological singularity': runaway self-improving AI rapidly surpassing and possibly endangering humanity.

p.619: chapter 20 begins with a review of the book's key concepts.

concepts.name: Blend of algorithmic and geometric modules
concepts.definition: Models combining algorithmic modules (formal reasoning, search, abstraction) with geometric modules (intuition, pattern recognition).
concepts.technical: Realizes both value-centric and program-centric abstraction; today exemplified (with hand-coded algorithmic parts) by AlphaGo and self-driving cars.
concepts.misconception: That the existing examples are already the vision. They required much manual engineering.

concepts.name: Global library of reusable subroutines
concepts.definition: A library of modular parts evolved by learning high-performing models on thousands of tasks, from which new models are grown.
concepts.intuition: An ever-growing standard library written by AIs.
concepts.technical: Frequent problem-solving patterns identified by the meta-learner become subroutines, like functions and classes.
concepts.significance: Point 3 of the vision; the store of reusable knowledge enabling data-efficient learning.
concepts.example: A 'detect enemies' subroutine reused across video games.
concepts.misconception: That it's curated by humans. It's evolved automatically.

concepts.name: Program synthesis guided by program-space intuition
concepts.definition: Discrete search over combinations of subroutines, heavily guided by deep learning.
concepts.intuition: A search that knows where to look.
concepts.technical: Discrete search produces exact, non-differentiable program structure; a learned model ranks candidates to tame combinatorial explosion.
concepts.significance: Point 4 of the vision; the 'engine' that grows models.
concepts.example: Choosing which three library subroutines to chain for a new puzzle, with a network ranking candidates.
concepts.misconception: That deep learning will do the search itself end to end. It guides a discrete search.

concepts.name: Human-like extreme generalization
concepts.definition: Assembling a working model for a new task or situation from very little data.
concepts.intuition: Learning a new video game in minutes thanks to experience with other games.
concepts.technical: Enabled by program-like primitives that generalize well plus experience with similar tasks; contrasts with stimulus-action mappings.
concepts.significance: Point 5 of the vision and the chapter's definition of the goal.
concepts.example: The video-game example on this page.
concepts.misconception: That it comes from memorizing more examples. It comes from abstract, program-like models.

concepts.name: Artificial general intelligence (as framed here)
concepts.definition: A perpetually learning model-growing system with human-like generalization.
concepts.intuition: A system that keeps getting better at learning new things.
concepts.technical: Defined functionally by its adaptive, model-building capacity, not by goals or consciousness.
concepts.significance: Closes the chapter; the authors reject singularitarian apocalypse narratives as fantasy.
concepts.example: The library + meta-learner system of figure 19.16, run perpetually.
concepts.misconception: That AGI implies a robot apocalypse. The authors call this pure fantasy.

deeper.title: Each point of the vision, traced back to its subsection
deeper.body:
| Vision point (pp.617-618) | Where it was developed |
|---|---|
| 1. Models more like programs, closer to mental models | 19.1.3 (p.593) limits; 19.4.3 (p.612); 19.4.4 (p.613) program synthesis |
| 2. Blend of algorithmic and geometric modules | 19.4.1-19.4.2 (pp.609-611); 19.4.5 hybrids (pp.614-615) |
| 3. Grown from a global library of subroutines | 19.4.6 (pp.616-617), figure 19.16 |
| 4. Discrete search guided by deep learning intuition | 19.4.5 second avenue (pp.615-616) |
| 5. Human-like extreme generalization | 19.2.2 (p.597); ARC (pp.605-607) |

Using this table, you can review the whole of chapter 19 from its conclusion backward.

deeper.title: Why a richer library makes search cheaper, not harder
deeper.body: Beyond the book: suppose a task needs 12 low-level operations from 30 primitives: about $30^{12} \approx 5\times10^{17}$ flat candidates. If the library contains abstract subroutines such that the same behavior is 3 calls drawn from 1,000 subroutines, the space is $1000^3 = 10^9$, smaller by eight orders of magnitude, even before learned guidance. Abstraction shortens programs, and shortness matters more than vocabulary size. This is one way to understand why the vision pairs a growing library with guided search.

deeper.title: Analogy: the video-game player
deeper.body: The page's own example, expanded: a novice who learned one platformer by memorizing 'jump at the third pit' has a stimulus-action map useless elsewhere. A veteran has internalized concepts like 'hazards', 'checkpoints', 'enemy patrol patterns', and 'try, observe, adjust'. These are reusable subroutines. Facing a new game, the veteran fetches the relevant ones, composes a plan, and adapts after a few attempts: a human version of figure 19.16.

misconceptions.claim: In the vision, deep learning is replaced by symbolic AI.
misconceptions.correction: Geometric (deep learning) modules remain, both inside models and as the guide for program search.

misconceptions.claim: AlphaGo and self-driving cars already realize the vision.
misconceptions.correction: They are early examples of the blend, but required a lot of manual software engineering and human design decisions; the vision has models grown automatically.

misconceptions.claim: Human skill at new video games comes from a basic mapping between stimuli and action.
misconceptions.correction: The book says it comes from abstract, program-like models derived from previous experience.

misconceptions.claim: The authors predict AGI will lead to a singularity.
misconceptions.correction: They explicitly call a singularitarian robot apocalypse pure fantasy.

takeaways: Future models will be program-like and generalize better thanks to their algorithmic nature.
They will blend algorithmic and geometric modules, i.e., program-centric and value-centric abstraction.
They will be grown automatically from a global library of subroutines evolved over thousands of tasks.
Growing them will use discrete program synthesis guided by deep-learning intuition.
The goal is human-like extreme generalization from little data; the authors call the result a form of AGI but reject singularity fantasies.

questions.question: In the long-term vision, what kind of process searches over combinations of subroutines to grow new models?
options: Discrete search (program synthesis) heavily guided by deep-learning intuition
questions.answer: Discrete search (program synthesis) heavily guided by deep-learning intuition
questions.explanation: Stated in the fourth bullet. Gradient descent alone can't search discrete structures, unguided search explodes combinatorially (p.615), and the vision explicitly removes manual design.

questions.question: According to the page, why can humans quickly learn a complex new video game?
questions.answer: Because experience with many previous games yields models that are abstract and program-like rather than a basic mapping between stimuli and action.
questions.explanation: This is the book's analogy for extreme generalization in the fifth bullet.

questions.question: Which two kinds of abstraction does the blend of algorithmic and geometric modules achieve, and which module provides which?
questions.answer: Program-centric abstraction (algorithmic modules: formal reasoning, search, abstraction) and value-centric abstraction (geometric modules: informal intuition, pattern recognition).
questions.explanation: From the second bullet, using the vocabulary of 19.4.1.

questions.question: Give the two reasons the system can assemble a working model for a new task with very little data.
questions.answer: Rich program-like primitives that generalize well, and extensive experience with similar tasks.
questions.explanation: Both are named in the fifth bullet.

questions.question: What is the authors' stance on a 'singularitarian robot apocalypse'?
options: It is an inevitable consequence of AGI
It is a serious risk the book analyzes in detail
It is pure fantasy stemming from misunderstandings of intelligence and technology
questions.answer: It is pure fantasy stemming from misunderstandings of intelligence and technology
questions.explanation: The final paragraph says this and adds that a fuller critique doesn't belong in the book, so it's neither analyzed in detail nor predicted.

questions.question: How do frequent problem-solving patterns end up in the global library?
questions.answer: The meta-learning system identifies them and turns them into reusable subroutines, like functions and classes in software engineering, which are added to the library.
questions.explanation: Third bullet; matches the push arrow in figure 19.16 (p.617).

questions.question: Can you restate the five points of the long-term vision from memory and name the earlier subsection that developed each?
questions.answer: Program-like models (19.4.3-19.4.4); algorithmic + geometric blend (19.4.1-19.4.2, 19.4.5); grown from a global library (19.4.6); guided discrete search (19.4.5); extreme generalization (19.2.2, 19.3).
